Hello and.. I am a Master's student from University of Waterloo, and I have some Polylogarithms problem Set (which is also formalized into Lean4) with 16 questions, the definitions and property/identities, and here's the link of the repo: https://github.com/rainrzk/LeanPolyLog - including:

  • power series；Li_s(z) = Σ_{n≥1} zⁿ/nˢ
  • derivative；Li_{s+1}′(z) = Li_s(z)/z
  • continuity；closed unit disk |z| ≤ 1
  • duplication formula；Li_s(z²) = 2^{s−1}(Li_s(z) + Li_s(−z))
  • reflection formula；Li₂(x) + Li₂(1−x) = π²/6 − log x · log(1−x), 0 < x < 1
  • Landen's identity；Li₂(z) + Li₂(z/(z−1)) = −½ log²(1−z), |z| ≤ 1, Re z ≤ ½
  • ∫₀^{π/2} log²(sin x) dx = π³/24 + (π/2) log² 2

(I have to claim that the original proof was wrote by myself, but the work Lean4 formalization work was made by Claude)

Is there already some work here for polylogarithms (that might decide whether I duplicate same work or not) and does this also need a PR similar to what #26172 did?
Polylogarithms might have to wait for the Lerch transcendent to be defined – the latter has as special cases both polylogarithms and the already-in-mathlib Hurwitz zeta function

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lerch_transcendent

This is just the kind of comment which might be the right idea but which might derail progress in practice. Ideally we would have a definitive answer to "does mathlib want this function or is it something nobody cares about any more" (and I don't know the answer). Whose job is it to answer this question? We certainly want poly logarithms!
Yes, we can certainly ignore Lerch and just define polylogarithms right away

Thanks for sharing your ideas and the Lerch transcendent!

My feeling is that these questions are not mathematical but sociological, and depend on how the functions are used in practice. I've not fact-checked the below by the way, so it relies on my unreliable memory. I think that for real square roots of negative reals mathlib changed its mind at some point (sqrt(-x) changed from 0 to sqrt(x) IIRC) and for inverse trig functions I think we just followed what Isabelle/HOL did. So you could look for prior work, perhaps in other provers. But at the end of the day junk values are supposed to make it easier for the user (the reason 1/0=0 and not 37 is because a/c+b/c=(a+b)/c always) so if there are theorems which come out easier with some choices of junk value than others then perhaps this is an indication of what you should be doing. But at the end of the day I don't think that not knowing the best junk value should hold back making a development -- make a choice and go with it, you'll find out soon enough if you could have made a better one.
